places.name: Taishan Cuisine
places.desc: Taishan (=Toisan, autonym Hoisan) is the region of Guangdong Province that was the early source of much of San Francisco's Chinese population, and this restaurant is the best Taishanese restaurant in town. Famous for their yellow-eel rice clay pot, roast chicken, 5-spice duck, frogs legs, and cauliflower with preserved pork. Also open very late (3am?) for those of you who are jet-lagged.

places.name: R & G Lounge
places.desc: Classic Cantonese seafood (salt-and-pepper crab, Cantonese clear-steamed fish, or black cod).

places.name: Capital
places.desc: Probably the best crispy salt-and-pepper wings you will eat this year. Also other standard Cantonese fare.

places.name: Four Kings 四大天王
places.desc: SF Chronicle's #1 resto in SF. Elevated Cantonese. Hard to get into but you can sometimes succeed if you wait in line before they open.

places.name: Lai Hong Lounge
places.desc: Classic HK-style dimsum. Possibly the last place that still uses carts, at least on the weekend.

places.name: Hon’s Wun-Tun House 洪記面家
places.desc: Best HK wonton noodles in town. Very busy.

places.name: Palette Tea House
places.desc: High-end dim sum by the owner of Koi Palace. (In Ghirardelli Square, on the beautiful waterfront and an early (1962) case of adaptive reuse that turned a brick chocolate factory into shops.)

places.name: Harborview Restaurant & Bar
places.desc: Cantonese, dimsum and also dinner, amazing views.

places.name: Yuet Lee Seafood Restaurant
places.desc: Classic late-nite Hong Kong-style Cantonese food (well, these days just til 11pm).

places.name: The Happy Crane
places.desc: The latest hot place. Cantonese meets molecular gastronomy. Hard to get into.

places.name: Cantoo Latin Asian Rotisserie
places.desc: Venezuelan Chinese! Gritty part of the neighborhood.

places.desc: US spinoff of Tokyo brand. Gritty part of the neighborhood.
